extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalism students, researchers, and practitioners interested in citizen journalism
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of citizen journalism: definitions, theoretical elements, types, historical examples, criticisms, legal issues, and observed characteristics that shape how citizen-produced news is evaluated and practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory practice / community involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism is based upon members of the community playing an active role in the process of collecting, reporting, analyzing, and disseminating news and information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that ordinary people — not professional journalists — can be the main creators and distributors of news. Examples include eyewitness accounts, local residents writing local news, mobile-phone photos and videos uploaded to platforms. Evaluate contributions by the degree of active community engagement and whether the actor is genuinely a member of the covered community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of journalistic practices vs different objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism 'uses similar journalistic practices but is driven by different objectives and ideals and relies on alternative sources of legitimacy than traditional or mainstream journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether content follows recognizable journalistic methods (reporting, sourcing, verification) even when motivated by activism, advocacy, or community goals. Consider how legitimacy is established (peer recognition, social sharing, platform policies) rather than institutional credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition / scope (distinguish from related forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism should not be confused with community journalism, civic journalism, collaborative journalism, or social journalism — each denotes different mixes of professional/non-professional participation or editorial control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing work, be explicit about which form is intended (pure citizen-produced content, collaborative projects with professionals, professionally run social journalism, etc.) to set expectations for standards and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local embeddedness and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism is 'highly embedded in local communities' where residents engage in everyday storytelling about local politics, public affairs, community events, neighbourhood issues, schools, public transport, land use and environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value is often in proximity and local knowledge. Evaluate reporting for depth of local context, relevance to community stakeholders, and ability to surface issues overlooked by mainstream outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and platform enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism was made more feasible by online internet platforms, social networking, media-sharing websites and the prevalence of cellular telephones; these technologies made citizen journalism more accessible worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how platform affordances (ease of publishing, multimedia support, distribution algorithms) enable speed, reach, and engagement. Consider platform-specific constraints (moderation, algorithmic demotion) when judging effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed / timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to technology, citizens often can report breaking news more quickly than traditional media reporters; speed and space are identified as key characteristics of citizen journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timeliness as a positive criterion (first-hand, real-time reporting) but balance against verification needs; rapid reporting can increase impact (examples: 2010 Haiti earthquake, Arab Spring, Ferguson protests, George Floyd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness: open publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three elements critical to the rise of citizen journalism is open publishing (low barriers to publish content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate platforms and practices for how openly they allow contributions (anyone can publish) and how that openness affects volume, diversity, and the need for moderation/curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative editing / collective curation
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative editing is a core element enabling citizen journalism, where multiple contributors can edit, augment or fact-check media in collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presence and effectiveness of collaborative workflows (wiki-style editing, community moderation, crowdsourced verification). Anti-patterns include unmanaged edits that introduce errors or conflicts without resolution mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed content / decentralisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed content (multiple nodes of publication and distribution rather than single centralized gatekeepers) is a critical element of citizen journalism's rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge projects by how decentralised their publication/distribution is (many independent contributors, social sharing) and by whether decentralisation aids plurality of voices or causes fragmentation and misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and formats (audience participation vs platforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism appears in various forms: audience participation (comments, blogs, photos/video), independent news websites, participatory news sites, collaborative/contributory media, personal broadcasting sites, open-source news platforms, and thin media (mailing lists, newsletters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating work, consider format-specific expectations (e.g., a personal blog vs a participatory news site) — standards for sourcing, editing, and verification differ by format and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalists may also be activists within communities, and critics accuse proponents of abandoning the traditional goal of objectivity; citizen journalism can be heavily opinionated and subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate degree of bias and whether opinion is transparent. For accountability, mark advocacy clearly and separate factual reporting from commentary. Lack of objectivity is an anti-pattern when presented as neutral reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers have criticized citizen journalism for not having access to real-time fact checking; mainstream media sometimes misreports, but citizen reports also face verification challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence of sourcing, corroboration, and verification processes (multiple witnesses, metadata checks, cross-referencing). Platforms or projects with explicit verification workflows score higher on reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, professionalism and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalists are often portrayed as unreliable, biased and untrained compared to professionals who have recognition, paid work and journalistic training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contributors' competence (knowledge of reporting ethics, legal risks, verification techniques). Training or editorial mentorship programs are positive indicators; lack of skills is a common weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standards, curation and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Some citizen journalism sites improved editorially but often by not expensing editorial costs; many sites were initially lacking in quality and content, showing variable editorial oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of editorial policies, moderation, copyediting, and correction mechanisms. Anti-patterns include ghost-town sites with little moderation, or platforms that scale by foregoing editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs curation/aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of content produced by amateur news bloggers was not original content but curated information monitored and edited by bloggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate original reporting (eyewitness accounts, unique investigations) from aggregation/curation; both have value but should be labeled and held to different standards (attribution, added analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness, plurality and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism can surface voices otherwise unheard and reach audiences that mainstream outlets miss; it is theorized as a democratic response to corporate media concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether citizen journalism increases plurality (multiplicity and poly-centrality), includes marginalized perspectives, and avoids cherry-picking or reinforcing existing power imbalances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status, protections and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal repercussions: shield laws and reporter's privilege vary by jurisdiction and sometimes depend on whether a person is considered a 'journalist'; libel and court vulnerability are higher for unprofessional journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess awareness and compliance with local legal frameworks (defamation laws, privacy, criminalisation of recording in certain contexts). Projects should provide legal guidance for contributors and consider whether contributors qualify for shield-law protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, risk and potential repercussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalists may face detention, censorship, or other reprisals (examples: detained Wuhan journalist, Hong Kong protests' fake journalist packages); in some countries filming police was criminalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate safety protocols (operational security, anonymisation, backup of materials), risk disclosures, and platform responses to threats. Safety planning is essential in hostile environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial sustainability and resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Some citizen journalism ventures reached editorial improvements only by not expensing editorial costs; budget constraints affect professional capacity and influence the amount/quality of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess funding models, whether editorial work is resourced, and sustainability plans. Lack of resources is often linked to uneven coverage and editorial shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on traditional journalism and newsroom practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism's volume and speed have forced traditional journalists to compete, produce content faster, and sometimes incorporate citizen material; this has affected beats and newsroom workloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating citizen journalism's value, consider its influence on mainstream reporting, its utility as source material for professional outlets, and whether it complements or undermines journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic triad (speed & space; multiplicity & poly-centrality; interactivity & participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natalie Fenton associates citizen journalism with three characteristics: speed and space, multiplicity and poly-centrality, and interactivity and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triad as a high-level evaluative framework: timeliness and reach (speed & space); decentralised, multiple sources (multiplicity & poly-centrality); and two-way engagement between producers and audience (interactivity & participation).
